SME recovery: comparing the five cases with industry peers

Group 10

23 October 2026

1. What this adds to the report

The five cases all lost SME establishments between 2022 and 2024. The next question is whether the same industries also lost establishments elsewhere. That distinction changes the reason for selecting each case for closer review.

Three groups declined while their industry peers grew: CBD professional services, CBD construction and Southbank hospitality. CBD finance and administrative services also declined, but less sharply than their peers. Their importance comes from the size of their remaining historical gaps.

The comparisons describe differences in business presence. They do not measure the effect of COVID or predict the effect of a support programme.

2. Data and comparison method

We use the supplied CLUE file business-establishments-and-jobs-data-by-business-size-and-anzsic.csv. Small and Medium business categories are summed within each census year, precinct and ANZSIC division. These categories cover establishments with 1–199 jobs. Missing job counts do not affect the establishment totals.

For each case, its reference is the same industry in all other precincts. The focal precinct is excluded so it cannot influence its own benchmark. We pool the counts before calculating growth: a precinct with one business does not receive the same weight as one with hundreds.

# An example using the CBD professional-services case, 2022 to 2024.
# These quantities are rebuilt from the raw source by run_peer_review().
example <- recent[recent$case_rank == 1, ]
peer_growth <- example$peer_end / example$peer_start - 1
benchmark_count <- example$n_start * (1 + peer_growth)
observed_minus_benchmark <- example$n_end - benchmark_count

The CBD had 1,383 professional-services SMEs in 2022. Applying the +2.8% growth of professional services outside the CBD gives a comparison count of about 1,422 in 2024. The observed count was 1,338, about 84 below that reference. The reference is a descriptive calculation, not a forecast or an estimate of businesses lost because of a particular policy or event.

Comparisons use years at least two years apart. An absent precinct–industry–year cell stays unknown. Published peer totals are accompanied by a matched-peer check using only precincts observed in both years.

3. Recent change: three distinct local gaps

Group Local growth Peer growth Difference Observed minus benchmark
CBD professional services -3.3% +2.8% -6.1 pp -83.8
CBD finance and insurance -3.6% -10.3% +6.7 pp +37.0
CBD administrative services -9.9% -13.3% +3.5 pp +8.4
CBD construction -13.5% +13.9% -27.4 pp -30.4
Southbank hospitality -4.7% +9.0% -13.7 pp -29.0

The professional-services gap combines a large existing sector with recent underperformance. Construction has the widest percentage-point difference, but starts from a smaller count. Southbank hospitality moves in the opposite direction to hospitality elsewhere. Finance and administrative services need a different explanation: their decline is shared across precincts, and the CBD performed relatively better during this recent period.

The five cases together remain 876 SMEs below their 2019 counts. Their 114 net loss since 2022 is part of that historical gap; the two numbers must not be added together.

4. Was relative weakness already present before 2020?

CBD professional services grew more slowly than peers in both 2017–2019 (-6.5 pp) and 2022–2024 (-6.1 pp). This recent gap is not entirely new. Construction and Southbank hospitality were ahead of peers in the earlier window and behind them in the recent one.

Earlier windows give a mixed picture. Professional services underperformed in only three of eight non-overlapping pre-period comparisons from 2003–2005 to 2017–2019, and outperformed peers in 2020–2022. The alternate even-year pre-period scheme gives five of eight underperformances. We therefore describe weakness in the two selected windows without claiming an uninterrupted historical trend or a permanent structural break.

5. How much do the cases depend on our choices?

Recent-decline cutoff

The four scale cases are the largest 2019–2024 shortfalls among groups that also declined by at least 2% in 2022–2024. The fifth case is selected separately: the largest hospitality shortfall outside the CBD among continuing declines.

The same four scale cases appear with a 1%, 2% or 3% recent-decline cutoff. At 0%, CBD health care replaces construction. At 5%, only two of the four original scale cases remain. The 2% cutoff is a practical case-selection choice, not a test of statistical significance.

Recent decline cutoff Original four retained Same four cases
0% 3/4 No
1% 4/4 Yes
2% 4/4 Yes
3% 4/4 Yes
5% 2/4 No

Baseline year

Using 2018 changes the shortlist. North Melbourne professional services replaces CBD construction, and Docklands replaces Southbank as the hospitality contrast. The first three CBD cases remain. All original five still have fewer SMEs in 2024 than in either baseline year, but their ranking and gap sizes depend on that choice.

Group 2018 count 2019 count 2024 count Change from 2018 Change from 2019
CBD professional services 1822 1788 1338 -26.6% -25.2%
CBD finance and insurance 720 719 534 -25.8% -25.7%
CBD administrative services 391 381 219 -44.0% -42.5%
CBD construction 126 141 96 -23.8% -31.9%
Southbank hospitality 206 236 202 -1.9% -14.4%

This matters most for Southbank hospitality: 2024 is just 1.9% below 2018, compared with 14.4% below 2019. Its recent underperformance remains, but the size of its historical shortfall should be tied explicitly to the 2019 baseline. The complete alternative roster is exported in baseline_case_selection.csv.

Peer composition

Excluding the CBD as well as Southbank still leaves hospitality peers growing by +4.7%, compared with Southbank’s -4.7%. The local divergence is not explained solely by a strong CBD rebound.

Construction has one establishment in a newly observed peer cell in 2024. Using only peer precincts observed in both years reduces peer growth from 13.9% to 13.3%. It does not change the conclusion. Every exported comparison includes peer coverage and matched-peer growth so this can be checked directly.

6. What this means for the report

Use the peer comparison to explain why each case is important. Professional services, construction and Southbank hospitality show local underperformance against growing peers. Finance and administrative services show large remaining gaps within industries that also declined elsewhere.

This supports differentiated priorities for further investigation. It does not establish the causes of the gaps, identify individual business closures, or show which intervention would work. Those claims need additional evidence.

7. Reproducibility

The supplement is built by scripts/07_peer_comparison_review.R; it can also be sourced and run as run_peer_review(root, make_figures = TRUE). Tables and figures are written under outputs/*/final/deeper_review/. The source checksum and R session details are saved alongside them. The raw file is unchanged.

tests/test_peer_comparison_review.R independently recomputes comparisons, rankings and history from the raw CSV, and checks missing-cell behaviour, zero denominators and the two-year comparison rule. Run it with:

# From the repository root, in a terminal:
# Rscript tests/test_peer_comparison_review.R
sessionInfo()
